paragraphs.text: In conclusion, early convolutional layers tend to tolerate more pruning, while linear layers exhibit heightened sensitivity.

Figure 2: Layer-wise sparsity tolerance across three architectures: GNNNets on BBBP, Spline on Cora, and HGPSL on Proteins. Each segmented line represents a layer, with colors indicating sparsity levels from 0.0 (dense, no pruning) to 0.9(90% weights removed).
Figure 6: The Changing CPU Usage of Using Pruning Methods
Figure 8: The Memory Usage of Regularization

24 – 28 for extreme rates  \( \geq 1e2 \) . There is similar behavior for the Cora-Link dataset. The energy rises to 22 – 32 for rates less than 0.9 and increases to 77 at the rates of  \( 1e2 \)  and  \( 10e6 \) , but remains stable between 26 – 28 otherwise. In conclusion, energy generally increases with higher regularization but spikes at specific thresholds (e.g., 0.6 – 0.8 for BBBP). High rates(1.00 –  \( 10^{6} \) ) may reduce energy consumption. For datasets Proteins and Cora-Node, the energy consumption is more stable than the others.

In transitional rates (e.g., 0.7–0.8 in the BBBP), the model balances between overfitting and underfitting, leading to fluctuating gradients, slower convergence, and exacerbated issues like vanishing/exploding gradients in message passing on sparse graphs. This demands more computational effort from the optimizer. In extreme rates (e.g.,  \( \geq 1 \)  in Cora): Regularization dominates the loss (via terms like  \( \lambda/2 * ||W||^{2} \) ), causing disproportionately large/unstable gradients, flattened loss landscapes, and challenges in embedding/link prediction tasks. This amplifies repeated gradient computations, numerical stabilizations, and sparse operations. While analyzing all resources together, we identify that low-to-moderate rates less than 1e-2 preserve accuracy, while higher rates degrade accuracy. Very high rates ( \( \geq 1e2 \) ) may reduce resource usage, but at the cost of decreasing accuracy. The energy and CPU usage spike at mid-rates 0.1-0.9, suggesting inefficiency during aggressive regularization. The Proteins dataset shows minimal impact on resources. "In conclusion, optimal regularization rates balance accuracy preservation and resource efficiency, typically in the range of 1e-6 to 1e-2. Higher rates are detrimental to both performance and computational cost."

related_claims.content: Early convolutional layers exhibit tolerance to pruning even at high global sparsity targets.
Linear projection layers and final classifier MLPs exhibit greater sensitivity to pruning than early convolutional layers.
Memory usage and CPU/energy consumption showed non-monotonic, dataset- and sparsity-dependent patterns.
Global unstructured magnitude pruning on the Cora node classification setup shows accuracy recovering from values near 0.86 to 0.90 ± 0.01 after fine-tuning at certain pruning levels.
Aggressive regularization rates (≥ 0.1) may produce spikes in energy and CPU usage at intermediate values.
Very large regularization sometimes reduces resource consumption but at the cost of greatly reduced accuracy.
When followed by fine-tuning, fine-grained layer-wise pruning can recover or surpass baseline accuracy on the structurally sensitive node classification task on Cora.
A regularization rate in the range 10^{2}–10^{6} sometimes reduces resource consumption but at the cost of Cora node classification accuracy dropping to 0.14–0.28 at rates ≥ 0.1.
On the Proteins dataset, accuracy is 0.82 for regularization rates up to 10\^{-2}.
On the BBBP dataset, accuracy remains 0.84–0.85 for regularization rates up to 10\^{-3}.
On the Cora link prediction dataset, energy spikes to 77 J at regularization rates 10\^{2}–10\^{6}.
On the Cora node classification dataset, accuracy is 0.87–0.90 for regularization rates up to 10\^{-2}.
On the Cora link prediction dataset, accuracy declines gradually from 0.95 to 0.92 for regularization rates up to 10\^{-2}.

With the respective GNN models, modest regularization (regularization rates below approximately 1×10\^{-2}) preserves accuracy across four datasets (BBBP, Cora node classification, Cora link prediction, Proteins).
Aggressive regularization rates (≥ 0.1) cause sharp accuracy degradation across four datasets (BBBP, Cora node classification, Cora link prediction, Proteins).
For fine-grained pruning, energy consumption is higher than for global pruning at the sparsity values of 0.1–0.3.
For fine-grained pruning, energy consumption is higher than for global pruning at low-to-moderate sparsities.
For global pruning, CPU usage peaks at 70% sparsity across Cora node classification, Cora link prediction, BBBP, and Proteins.
For fine-grained pruning, CPU and energy consumption exhibit sharp spikes and bimodal profiles.
QAT-INT8 and DQ-INT8 achieve higher accuracy than A^{2}Q on the BBBP and Proteins datasets.
For global pruning, CPU usage peaks at 70% sparsity across datasets.

In the comparison of the two magnitude-based pruning methods applied to the GNN architectures (SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, GIN) and tasks (node classification on Cora, link prediction on Cora, graph classification on BBBP and Proteins), global unstructured pruning exhibits more consistent behavior across tasks than fine-grained layer-wise pruning.
Fine-grained pruning may yield better accuracy recovery than global pruning on some datasets.
On the two graph classification tasks on BBBP and Proteins, fine-grained pruning with fine-tuning does not recover baseline accuracy at high sparsity.

On the GIN graph-classification model, for the BBBP dataset, Quantization-Aware Training with INT8 (QAT-INT8) achieves accuracy and inference time similar to Degree-Quant with INT8, but higher energy than Degree-Quant with INT8.
Global pruning is more energy-efficient than fine-grained pruning at the sparsity values of 0.4–0.8.
QAT-INT8 and DQ-INT8 achieve the accuracies of 0.83 ± 0.01 on BBBP and 0.72 ± 0.01 on Proteins, higher than A^{2}Q's on the BBBP and Proteins datasets.
On tasks other than structurally sensitive tasks, fine-grained pruning with fine-tuning does not recover baseline accuracy at high sparsity.
Global pruning is more energy-efficient than fine-grained pruning at medium-to-high sparsities.

Layer-wise analysis of sparsity under global unstructured magnitude pruning applied to the GNN architectures (GNNNet on BBBP, SplineConv on Cora node classification, HGP-SL on Proteins) reveals heterogeneous sensitivity to pruning.
Fine-grained layer-wise pruning, when applied without fine-tuning, yields larger accuracy drops than global unstructured pruning.

In the experiments on SplineConv, NESS, HGP-SL, GNNNet, and GIN, and on Cora node classification, Cora link prediction, BBBP, and Proteins, reductions in parameter count from pruning did not translate into consistent decreases in inference time or memory usage.
